glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Chronicles begins with Adam and traces humanity through Noah’s sons to Abraham and his related families, setting Israel’s story inside the history of the whole human race before the book turns to Israel’s own sons.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chronicles was written for God’s people after the exile, who had lost their king and temple and needed to know where they still belonged (9:1–2). This chapter draws its names mainly from Genesis 5, 10–11, 25 and 36.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “And Abraham begot Isaac. The sons of Isaac were Esau and Israel.” (1 Chronicles 1:34, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The first word of Chronicles is a name: “Adam” (1:1). Before the writer says anything about David, the temple or the exile, he reaches back to the beginning of the human race. The God of Israel is the Creator of all people, and Israel’s story begins inside the story of the whole world. The families of Japheth, Ham and Shem fill the first part of the chapter, with brief notes about Nimrod, who “began to be a mighty one on the earth” (1:10), and Peleg, “for in his days the earth was divided” (1:19).

Then the record narrows. A second short line runs from Shem to “Abram, who is Abraham” (1:27), and from Abraham to Isaac, whose sons were “Esau and Israel” (1:34). Even as the line narrows, room is kept for Ishmael’s sons, Keturah’s sons, Esau’s family, the families of Seir and the kings of Edom. These related peoples are remembered before Israel’s sons appear in chapter 2.

For readers who had come through exile, this long roll of names carried a steady message. Kingdoms had fallen and the temple had been destroyed, yet the people to whom God had made His promises still stood in a history reaching back to Adam. Because the names record real people and real descent, that message rests on solid ground.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
1 Chronicles 1:1–4 — From Adam to Noah and His Sons

The record opens with ten generations from Adam to Noah and then names Noah’s three sons. This compressed line, drawn from Genesis 5, ties Israel’s history to the first man God made.

1 Chronicles 1:5–23 — The Families of Noah’s Sons

The families of Japheth, Ham and Shem are listed in the order of Genesis 10, with brief notices of Nimrod and of Peleg. The section places Israel’s ancestors among the peoples of the earth without ranking one family above another.

1 Chronicles 1:24–27 — From Shem to Abraham

A second short line runs from Shem through Eber, Peleg and Terah to Abram. The closing words, “Abram, who is Abraham” (1:27), recall the new name God gave him along with His promise.

1 Chronicles 1:28–34 — The Families of Abraham

Abraham’s sons Isaac and Ishmael are named, followed by Ishmael’s twelve sons and the sons of Keturah. The section returns to Isaac and ends with his two sons, Esau and Israel, preparing for the record of both families.

1 Chronicles 1:35–42 — The Families of Esau and Seir

Esau’s sons and grandsons through Eliphaz and Reuel are listed, then the families of Seir, the earlier inhabitants of the land where Esau settled. Genesis 36 keeps these Horite families distinct from Esau’s line while showing how the two were connected.

1 Chronicles 1:43–54 — The Kings and Chiefs of Edom

The kings who reigned in Edom “before a king reigned over the children of Israel” (1:43) are listed in order, followed by Edom’s chiefs. The notice quietly points ahead to Israel’s own kingship, which will fill much of Chronicles.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
This chapter tells us that the God of the Bible is the God of all peoples. Israel’s calling did not begin apart from the nations but among them, and Genesis 12:1–3 shows that God called Abraham with blessing for all the families of the earth in view. The chapter also shows that God works through real history and real families across long generations.

For people who wondered whether the exile had erased them, the list said that God had not lost track of His people. Christian readers will also notice that Luke traces the ancestry of Jesus back to Adam (Luke 3:38), placing the Savior within the same human family this chapter records.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
One human family. Every people in the list descends from Adam through Noah’s sons (1:1–23).

The narrowing line. The record moves from all the nations to Abraham, Isaac and Israel (1:24–34).

Related peoples remembered. Ishmael’s sons, Keturah’s sons, Esau and the families of Seir all receive a place (1:28–42).

Kingship anticipated. Edom had kings before Israel did, a detail that prepares for the book’s concern with Israel’s throne (1:43).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Genealogy. A record of descent that may select particular lines without naming every relative. In Chronicles these lists are true history arranged to show God’s people where they came from (1:1–54).

Nimrod. A son of Cush who “began to be a mighty one on the earth” (1:10). Chronicles gives only this brief notice; Genesis 10:8–12 tells more about him.

Peleg. His name is tied to the time when “the earth was divided” (1:19), best read alongside the scattering of the nations in Genesis 10–11.

“Abram, who is Abraham.” The name God gave him when He promised to make him a father of many nations (1:27; Genesis 17:5).

Edom and Seir. Edom is the nation descended from Esau. Seir is the mountain region south of the Dead Sea where Esau settled and where Horite families lived before him (1:35–54; Genesis 36:8, 20).

Israel. Chronicles calls Jacob by the name God gave him, so the man and the nation that came from him share one name (1:34; 2:1).

focus: Chapter 1 opens Chronicles by setting Israel’s ancestry within the history of all humanity. It traces humanity from Adam through Noah’s sons to Abraham, records Abraham’s related families, and then turns to Esau, Seir, and the kings and chiefs of Edom.

sections.title: From Adam to Noah and His Sons
sections.summary: The record begins with Adam and traces the line through Seth, Enoch, and Methuselah to Noah, naming his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

sections.title: The Families of Noah’s Sons
sections.summary: The descendants of Japheth, Ham, and Shem are listed, with brief notices of Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one on the earth, and of Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided.

sections.title: From Shem to Abraham
sections.summary: The line narrows from Shem through Eber, Peleg, and Terah to Abram, who is Abraham.

sections.title: The Families of Abraham
sections.summary: Abraham’s sons Isaac and Ishmael are named, followed by the sons of Ishmael and the sons born to Keturah. The section closes by returning to Isaac, whose sons were Esau and Israel.

sections.title: The Families of Esau and Seir
sections.summary: The sons of Esau and his sons Eliphaz and Reuel are listed, followed by the families of Seir.

sections.title: The Kings and Chiefs of Edom
sections.summary: The kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over the children of Israel are listed in succession, followed by the chiefs of Edom.

1.brief: Chronicles begins with Adam, then Seth and Enosh, tracing the line from the first man God created. Opening with Adam places Israel’s story within the history of all humanity and identifies Israel’s God as the Creator.
1.explain:
“Adam,”

First Chronicles opens with a single name and no introduction. There is no title, no setting, and no sentence, only “Adam.” For a people rebuilding their life after exile, the first word of the book reaches back to the very beginning. Adam was the first man, formed by God from the dust and given life by His breath (Genesis 2:7). By starting here, Chronicles places Israel's story inside the story of all humanity. Israel's God is not a local deity whose concern begins with one nation. He is the Creator of every human being, and the history Chronicles will tell belongs within His purposes for the whole world.

“Seth, Enosh,”

The list moves directly from Adam to “Seth,” the son born after Abel's death (Genesis 4:25), and then to Seth's son “Enosh.” Chronicles passes over Cain and Abel without mention. It is following the line that Genesis 5 traces from Adam to Noah, the line through which the narrative of Genesis continues. Genesis notes that in the days of Enosh “men began to call on the name of the LORD” (Genesis 4:26). Chronicles gives no such comment. The names stand on their own, and their bare listing asks the reader to receive them as real people in a real line of descent.
1.notes:
Verses 1–4 consist entirely of names, without connecting words such as “begot” or “the son of.” They compress Genesis 5 into thirteen names.

In Genesis 5 each generation from Adam to Lamech is given with ages, and the entries normally close with “and he died.” Enoch is the exception: “he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24). The chapter ends with Noah still living; his death is recorded in Genesis 9:29.

2.brief: The line continues through Cainan, Mahalalel, and Jared, following the descent recorded in Genesis 5. The names are given without narrative, presenting them as real generations in a continuing line of descent.
2.explain:
“Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared,”

The line continues through three more generations. “Cainan” was the son of Enosh, “Mahalalel” the son of Cainan, and “Jared” the son of Mahalalel (Genesis 5:9–18). Genesis tells us little about these men beyond their ages and the fact that each had sons and daughters and died. Chronicles tells us even less. Yet their place in the list matters. Each name is a link in an unbroken chain from the first man toward Noah, and through Noah toward Abraham and Israel. The genealogy treats them as historical people, not as symbols. Their lives were part of the history God was directing, even though nothing they did is recorded.
2.notes: The NKJV spells the name “Cainan” here and in Genesis 5:9, while some translations use ‘Kenan.’ This Cainan, son of Enosh, is a different person from the Cainan whom Luke lists between Arphaxad and Shelah (Luke 3:36).

3.brief: Enoch, Methuselah, and Lamech carry the line toward Noah. Chronicles names them without the stories or ages that Genesis supplies, keeping attention on the continuity of the line.
3.explain:
“Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech,”

The names carry the line closer to Noah. “Enoch” is the most remarkable figure in the Genesis list. Genesis says twice that he “walked with God,” and adds, “he was not, for God took him” (Genesis 5:24). “Methuselah” his son is remembered as the longest-lived man in Scripture (Genesis 5:27). “Lamech” was Noah's father (Genesis 5:28–29).

Chronicles mentions none of this. It does not stop to tell Enoch's story or to note Methuselah's great age. Its purpose here is to show continuity, not to tell individual stories. The reader who knows Genesis supplies the background; the reader who does not still learns that these men stood in the line of descent that led to Noah.
3.notes: This Lamech, the son of Methuselah in Seth's line, is a different man from Lamech the descendant of Cain, who boasted of violence (Genesis 4:18–24). Genesis also has two men named Enoch: Cain's son (Genesis 4:17) and Jared's son, who walked with God (Genesis 5:18–24). Chronicles follows only Seth's line.

4.brief: The first sequence ends with Noah and his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. These sons become the heads of the families of the nations listed in the verses that follow.
4.explain:
“Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.”

The first sequence ends with “Noah,” the man through whom God preserved humanity in the flood, and his three sons, “Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” The list names ten generations from Adam through Noah, as in Genesis 5. With Noah the human family begins again. Every nation listed in the following verses traces back to one of these three sons, as Genesis 10 records: “from these the nations were divided on the earth after the flood” (Genesis 10:32).

Shem, Ham, and Japheth were Noah's sons (Genesis 5:32; 10:1), although this verse simply lists their names after his without stating the relationship. The order “Shem, Ham, and Japheth” follows Genesis. In the verses that follow, however, Chronicles will treat the families in reverse order, Japheth first, then Ham, and finally Shem, so that the line leading to Abraham comes last and can be followed forward.
4.notes: The Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, adds the words ‘the sons of Noah’ before the three names, making the relationship explicit. The Hebrew text followed by the NKJV simply lists them.

5.brief: The sons of Japheth are named: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. This begins Japheth’s branch of humanity, following the order of Genesis 10.
5.explain:
“The sons of Japheth were”

The genealogy now turns from a single line to the families of the nations, beginning with “Japheth.” The expression “the sons of” introduces the peoples descended from him. In genealogies like this, “sons” can refer to individual sons, to the peoples who descended from them, or to both.

“Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.”

Seven names follow, matching Genesis 10:2 exactly. Several are known from later Scripture and from ancient history. “Madai” is the Hebrew name for the Medes, who later joined the Persians in conquering Babylon. “Javan” corresponds to the Ionians, a name that came to stand for the Greeks; Daniel speaks of “the kingdom of Greece” using this name (Daniel 8:21). “Magog,” “Meshech,” and “Tubal” appear together in Ezekiel's prophecy against Gog (Ezekiel 38:2). In general, Japheth's descendants are associated with peoples to the north and west of Israel. Chronicles records them without comment, but their presence at the head of the list shows that the nations far beyond Israel's horizon belong to the one human family God made.
5.notes:
Gomer is commonly identified with the Cimmerians. Tubal and Meshech are often associated with Tabal and the Mushki, peoples of Asia Minor named in Assyrian records.

These identifications vary in certainty, and the names do not form a precise map of modern nations.

6.brief: Gomer’s sons are Ashkenaz, Diphath, and Togarmah. The record follows one of Japheth’s lines into the next generation.
6.explain:
“The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Diphath, and Togarmah.”

Chronicles follows one of Japheth's sons into the next generation. “Gomer” had three sons. “Ashkenaz” appears in Jeremiah as a kingdom summoned against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:27). “Togarmah” is mentioned in Ezekiel as a people trading horses and mules with Tyre and as an ally of Gog (Ezekiel 27:14; 38:6). “Diphath” is otherwise unknown. Chronicles traces only Gomer's and Javan's lines among Japheth's sons, just as Genesis does. The names remind the reader that God knew these distant peoples by name long before Israel encountered them.
6.notes:
Genesis 10:3 reads “Riphath” instead of “Diphath.” In Hebrew script the letters for d and r look very similar, and the difference is best explained as a copying variation. Many manuscripts of Chronicles and the ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint read “Riphath.”

In medieval Jewish tradition “Ashkenaz” became a name for Germany and gave rise to the term “Ashkenazi” for Jews of central and eastern Europe. This later usage does not determine the identity of the ancient people.

7.brief: Javan’s sons are Elishah, Tarshishah, Kittim, and Rodanim. Japheth’s descendants spread to peoples that Genesis 10:5 associates with the coastlands.
7.explain:
“The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshishah, Kittim, and Rodanim.”

The second line traced from Japheth is “Javan,” associated with the Greeks. His four sons are linked with peoples and places around the Mediterranean. “Kittim” is commonly identified with Cyprus; the NKJV translates the same Hebrew name as ‘Cyprus’ in passages such as Isaiah 23:1 and Daniel 11:30. “Tarshishah” corresponds to Tarshish, a distant seaport famous for ships and trade, the place to which Jonah tried to flee (Jonah 1:3). “Rodanim” is often connected with the island of Rhodes. “Elishah” is less certain but is also associated with the Mediterranean. Genesis says of these peoples, “From these the coastland peoples of the Gentiles were separated into their lands” (Genesis 10:5). Israel, a small nation in the hills of Canaan, was reminded that the God who called them also knew the peoples of the islands and distant seas.
7.notes: Genesis 10:4 reads “Tarshish” and “Dodanim.” “Tarshishah” is a variant form of the same name. “Rodanim” and “Dodanim” differ again by the similar Hebrew letters d and r. In Genesis 10:4, the ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint uses the spelling with r (‘Rhodians’), agreeing with Chronicles.

8.brief: The sons of Ham are Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Ham’s branch includes peoples well known in Israel’s later history, including Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt, and Canaan.
8.explain:
“The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.”

The genealogy turns to Ham's descendants. His four sons represent peoples who loomed large in Israel's history. “Cush” refers to the region south of Egypt along the upper Nile, often translated “Ethiopia” in English Bibles. “Mizraim” is the ordinary Hebrew name for Egypt, the land where Israel had been enslaved. “Put” is usually connected with Libya or a people near Egypt. “Canaan” is the ancestor of the peoples who lived in the land God later gave to Israel. The list names Israel's former oppressor and the inhabitants of the promised land in the same breath, as members of one human family descended from Noah.

9.brief: Cush’s sons are listed, together with the sons of Raama, Sheba and Dedan. The genealogy follows Ham’s descendants into a further generation of related peoples.
9.explain:
“The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raama, and Sabtecha.”

The record follows Cush into the next generation. His five sons are generally associated with peoples in Africa and across the Red Sea in Arabia. “Seba” is mentioned with Sheba as a distant land that would bring gifts to the king (Psalm 72:10). “Havilah” appears elsewhere in Genesis as a region (Genesis 2:11; 25:18). The names “Sabta” and “Sabtecha” are otherwise little known.

“The sons of Raama were Sheba and Dedan.”

The line continues through “Raama” to his sons “Sheba” and “Dedan,” peoples known for trade in Arabia. The queen who later visited Solomon came from Sheba (1 Kings 10:1). The genealogy follows these trading peoples without comment, but their inclusion shows how widely the human family had spread and how many peoples Israel would encounter through commerce and history.
9.notes:
Sheba and Dedan appear again as sons of Jokshan, Abraham's son by Keturah (1:32), and another Sheba appears among Joktan's sons in Shem's line (1:22).

The same names occur in different branches, possibly because tribal groups intermarried or settled together in Arabia, or because names were reused. The lists record these relationships without explaining them.

Genesis 10:7 reads “Sabtah,” “Raamah,” and “Sabtechah.” These are spelling variants.

10.brief: Cush fathered Nimrod, who began to be a mighty one on the earth. This brief notice marks Nimrod’s prominence without offering a full portrait of his character, for which Genesis 10:8–12 supplies more background.
10.explain:
“Cush begot Nimrod;”

The list pauses on one man. “Nimrod” is named as a descendant of “Cush.” “Begot” can refer to a direct father-son relationship or to more distant descent; Genesis gives no further detail.

“he began to be a mighty one on the earth.”

This brief notice interrupts the list to describe Nimrod's prominence. “A mighty one” describes a man of strength, power, and prominence. “He began” introduces his rise to prominence. Genesis adds that he was “a mighty hunter before the LORD” and that his kingdom began in Babel and Shinar and extended to Assyria, where he built Nineveh (Genesis 10:9–11). Chronicles repeats only the first statement. It records Nimrod's power without telling his whole story or giving a moral verdict. The notice shows that the rise of great powers belongs to the history God was recording, a history that would later include the empires of Assyria and Babylon, which conquered Israel and Judah.
10.notes:
Nimrod’s character is debated. Josephus (Antiquities 1.113–114) portrays him as a tyrant who urged the building of the tower, and Augustine (City of God 16.4) reads him as a hunter ‘against’ the Lord and calls him the founder of Babylon.

Genesis does not explicitly connect Nimrod with the tower, and the phrase “before the LORD” (Genesis 10:9) can be read positively or negatively. Chronicles’ brief notice does not settle the question.

Micah 5:6 sets “the land of Nimrod” in parallel with “the land of Assyria.”

11.brief: Mizraim’s descendants begin with Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, and Naphtuhim. These plural names describe peoples associated with Mizraim rather than single individuals.
11.explain:
“Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,”

Chronicles returns to Ham's second son, “Mizraim,” Egypt. The names that follow end in -im, the Hebrew plural, showing that they describe peoples or clans rather than individual sons. “Begot” here expresses the origin of peoples, not a single birth. “Ludim” may be a people in Africa, distinct from Lud in Shem's line (1:17). “Lehabim” may be connected with the Libyans. “Naphtuhim” has been associated with the Nile Delta region. “Anamim” is otherwise unknown. The list treats these groups as part of Egypt's family, showing how the peoples of northeast Africa were related in the ancient understanding preserved in Genesis 10:13–14.

12.brief: The list of Mizraim’s descendants ends with Pathrusim and Casluhim, adding that the Philistines and the Caphtorim came from them. The note places the Philistines, later Israel’s great enemy, within the one human family.
12.explain:
“Pathrusim, Casluhim”

Two more peoples complete the list of Mizraim's descendants. “Pathrusim” refers to the people of Pathros, a name for Upper Egypt in the south (Isaiah 11:11; Jeremiah 44:1). “Casluhim” is otherwise unknown.

“(from whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim).”

The parenthesis adds a note of great significance for Israel's later history. “The Philistines” were to become Israel's fiercest enemy in the days of Saul and David. Here they are placed in the family of nations descended from Noah. “The Caphtorim” were the people of Caphtor, usually identified with Crete or the Aegean region. The note does not single the Philistines out for condemnation. It simply records their origin, reminding Israel that even its enemies were part of the human family God made and governs.
12.notes:
Other passages link the Philistines with Caphtor (Amos 9:7; Jeremiah 47:4; compare Deuteronomy 2:23, where the Caphtorim come from Caphtor). For this reason several commentators prefer to place the parenthetical note after “Caphtorim” rather than after “Casluhim” (so the NET Bible’s note on Genesis 10:14).

Chronicles closely parallels Genesis 10:14. The two passages differ slightly in wording in the NKJV, but both place the Philistine-origin notice after Casluhim and include Caphtorim within its parentheses.

The list may reflect migration rather than family descent, though the evidence does not settle the details.

13.brief: Canaan’s descendants begin with Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth. These names point to peoples who later lived in and around the land promised to Israel.
13.explain:
“Canaan begot Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth;”

The record now turns to Ham's fourth son, “Canaan,” whose descendants occupied the land later promised to Israel. “Sidon, his firstborn” gave his name to the great Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel. “Heth” is the ancestor of the Hittites; Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah from “the sons of Heth” (Genesis 23:3). The list that begins here, continuing through verse 16, names peoples whom Israel would meet, fight, and sometimes live alongside in the land. Their inclusion shows that Israel's later conflicts with these peoples were conflicts within the one human family.
13.notes: The Hittites of Canaan in Genesis may be distinct from the great Hittite empire of Anatolia (modern Turkey), or may be an offshoot of it. The relationship is debated. In the biblical narratives, the “sons of Heth” or Hittites appear as one of the peoples of Canaan (Genesis 23:3; 26:34).

14.brief: The Jebusite, the Amorite, and the Girgashite are listed among Canaan’s descendants. These are peoples Israel would later encounter when it entered the land.
14.explain:
“the Jebusite, the Amorite, and the Girgashite;”

From this point, Hebrew uses singular expressions such as “the Jebusite” to refer to whole peoples, a common way of naming a people in that language. “The Jebusite” refers to the inhabitants of Jebus, the city later captured by David and made his capital, Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 11:4). “The Amorite” was one of the largest and most widespread peoples of Canaan, often used as a name for the land's inhabitants generally. “The Girgashite” is a smaller group named in the lists of Canaan's peoples (Joshua 3:10). For readers of Chronicles, the mention of the Jebusites would recall that the city at the center of their worship had once belonged to Canaan's descendants before God gave it to David.
14.notes: The peoples of Canaan often appear in lists of six or seven in the Pentateuch and Joshua (for example, Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 7:1; Joshua 3:10). Genesis 10:15–18 and 1:13–16 instead name eleven descendants of Canaan, a list that includes northern peoples and does not include the Perizzites.

15.brief: The Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite are added to Canaan’s line. Chronicles reproduces the record of Genesis 10 in compressed form, listing these clans without comment.
15.explain:
“the Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite;”

Three more Canaanite peoples are named. “The Hivite” inhabited several towns in Canaan; the Gibeonites who deceived Joshua were Hivites (Joshua 9:7). “The Arkite” and “the Sinite” are usually associated with towns in the region of Phoenicia, along the coast of modern Lebanon. Chronicles reproduces the list of Genesis 10:17 without comment. These peoples are remembered not for any deeds but simply because they belong to the family of nations.

16.brief: The list of Canaan’s descendants closes with the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite. With these names the record of Ham’s family is complete, and the genealogy turns to Shem.
16.explain:
“the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite.”

The list of Canaan's descendants ends with three peoples from the northern regions. “The Arvadite” came from Arvad, an island city off the Phoenician coast whose men served as sailors and soldiers for Tyre (Ezekiel 27:8, 11). “The Zemarite” is associated with a town in the same region. “The Hamathite” refers to the people of Hamath, a city on the Orontes River in Syria that later marked the northern ideal boundary of Israel's territory (1 Chronicles 13:5). With these names, the record of Ham's family is complete, and the genealogy turns to Shem.

17.brief: The sons of Shem are listed: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, Aram, Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. The record gathers Shem’s wider family, including names that Genesis 10:22–23 places within Aram’s branch, before the line narrows toward Abraham.
17.explain:
“The sons of Shem were”

The genealogy now reaches Shem, the son whose line will lead to Abraham. Genesis calls him “the father of all the children of Eber” (Genesis 10:21), anticipating the line that will be followed in verses 18–27.

“Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, Aram,”

The first five names match Genesis 10:22. “Elam” was a people east of Babylon, in what is now southwestern Iran. “Asshur” is the ancestor of Assyria, the empire that later destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel. “Arphaxad” is the son through whom the line to Abraham runs. “Lud” is uncertain. “Aram” is the ancestor of the Arameans, the peoples of Syria with whom Israel had long dealings. Abraham's relatives in Haran lived among the Arameans (Genesis 25:20).

“Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.”

The last four names are listed as though they were also Shem's sons. Genesis 10:23 identifies them as “the sons of Aram,” that is, Shem's grandsons through Aram. Chronicles compresses the list, gathering the whole of Shem's wider family together before narrowing to one line. “Uz” is the name of the land where Job lived (Job 1:1). The genealogy shows that Shem's descendants spread into many peoples, among whom Israel's ancestors were only one family.
17.notes:
The Hebrew text of Chronicles lacks the words “the sons of Aram” before Uz (compare Genesis 10:23), while some manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint include them.

Either the compression is intentional, treating the grandsons together with the sons, or the phrase dropped out in copying, perhaps when a copyist’s eye skipped from one occurrence of “Aram” to the next. The NKJV translates the Hebrew of Chronicles as it stands.

Genesis 10:23 reads “Mash” instead of “Meshech,” and the ancient Syriac translation and a few Hebrew manuscripts of Chronicles also read ‘Mash.’ This Meshech in Shem’s line is a different person from Meshech the son of Japheth (1:5).

18.brief: Arphaxad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber. One family is singled out from Shem’s sons and followed forward.
18.explain:
“Arphaxad begot Shelah, and Shelah begot Eber.”

From all of Shem's family, the record now follows one line. “Arphaxad” fathered “Shelah,” and Shelah fathered “Eber.” The verse uses the word “begot” for each step, drawing attention to direct succession. Eber is an important name. Genesis singles out Shem as “the father of all the children of Eber” (Genesis 10:21), and many see a connection between Eber's name and the word “Hebrew,” the name by which Abraham's descendants were later known. Whether or not that connection is intended, Eber stands as a key ancestor in the line leading to Abraham.
18.notes:
The ancient Greek translation of Genesis known as the Septuagint (Genesis 10:24; Genesis 11:12–13) and Luke's genealogy include an additional generation, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Shelah (Luke 3:36). The Hebrew text of both Genesis and Chronicles names Arphaxad as Shelah's father directly.

Genesis 10:24 and 11:12 in the NKJV read “Salah” for the name spelled “Shelah” here.

The proposed link rests on shared consonants in the Hebrew name Eber (’ever) and the Hebrew word for “Hebrew” (’ivri). The text itself does not make that connection. Genesis 14:13, where Abram is called “the Hebrew,” is the first use of the term.

19.brief: Eber has two sons: Peleg, so named because the earth was divided in his days, and his brother Joktan. The notice about Peleg recalls the division of peoples in Genesis 10–11 and does not offer a scientific account of the continents.
19.explain:
“To Eber were born two sons:”

Eber's family divides into two branches. The verse follows Genesis 10:25 word for word.

“the name of one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided;”

The name “Peleg” sounds like the Hebrew verb meaning ‘to divide.’ The explanation is given in the verse itself: “in his days the earth was divided.” In the context of Genesis 10–11, “the earth” most naturally refers to the peoples of the earth, and the division points to the scattering of humanity at Babel, when the LORD confused their language and “scattered them abroad over the face of all the earth” (Genesis 11:8–9). Genesis 10 repeatedly speaks of peoples being divided or separated by their lands and languages (Genesis 10:5, 32). Peleg's name preserved the memory of that division.

“and his brother's name was Joktan.”

Peleg's brother “Joktan” is named, and the next verses list Joktan's sons. The line to Abraham, however, runs through Peleg (1:25). The two brothers represent the two directions of Eber's family: one branch spreads into many peoples, and the other narrows toward Abraham.
19.notes: The Hebrew name Peleg and the Hebrew verb palag, “to divide,” share the same main letters: p, l, and g. This connects his name with the statement that the earth “was divided” in his days.

20.brief: Joktan’s sons begin with Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, and Jerah. The record follows Joktan’s family before returning to Peleg’s line.
20.explain:
“Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,”

Before following Peleg's line, the record lists Joktan's descendants, as Genesis 10:26–29 does. Joktan had thirteen sons, and the list runs through verse 23. Most of these names are associated with peoples and places in southern Arabia. “Hazarmaveth” is commonly connected with Hadramaut, a region in what is now Yemen. “Almodad,” “Sheleph,” and “Jerah” are less certain. Chronicles gives Joktan's family its place in history even though the main story will not follow them.

21.brief: Hadoram, Uzal, and Diklah continue the list of Joktan’s sons, the branch of Eber’s family that runs alongside Peleg’s line.
21.explain:
“Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,”

Three more of Joktan's sons are named. “Uzal” has been associated with a place in southern Arabia, though the identification is uncertain. “Hadoram” and “Diklah” are otherwise unknown. Joktan's branch runs alongside Peleg's, and its record shows that Eber's descendants were not limited to Abraham's family. These names are remembered because they belong to the human family God made and knows, whether or not their later history is recorded in Scripture.

22.brief: Ebal, Abimael, and Sheba are added to Joktan’s family. This Sheba descends from Shem and is distinct from Sheba the son of Raama, a descendant of Ham, in verse 9.
22.explain:
“Ebal, Abimael, Sheba,”

The list of Joktan's sons continues. “Sheba” here is a descendant of Shem through Joktan, distinct from Sheba the son of Raama in Ham's line (1:9). Both names are associated with Arabian peoples, and the kingdom of Sheba in southern Arabia may have included people from more than one branch. “Ebal” and “Abimael” are otherwise unknown. The list preserves each name without explanation.
22.notes: Genesis 10:28 reads “Obal” for “Ebal.” The difference is a small variation in vowels and consonants between the two texts. This Ebal is unrelated to the son of Shobal in Seir's family (1:40) or to Mount Ebal in Israel.

23.brief: Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab complete the list, and the verse sums up that all these were the sons of Joktan. Shem’s descendants spread into many peoples, not only the line that leads to Abraham.
23.explain:
“Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab.”

Three final names complete Joktan's family. “Ophir” was famous in Israel as a source of fine gold. Solomon's ships brought gold from Ophir (1 Kings 9:28), and a royal psalm pictures the queen standing “in gold from Ophir” (Psalm 45:9), the finest gold of the day. “Havilah” shares its name with a son of Cush (1:9), again showing that some names appear in more than one branch. “Jobab” here is a different person from the Edomite king Jobab (1:44).

“All these were the sons of Joktan.”

The summary closes Joktan's branch. Shem's descendants had spread into many peoples. The record honors them as part of the human family before narrowing its focus to one line.
23.notes: Ophir’s location is uncertain. Southern Arabia, the African coast, and India have all been proposed.

24.brief: A second, compressed line begins with Shem, Arphaxad, and Shelah. Restarting with Shem narrows the focus from the nations to one particular line.
24.explain:
“Shem, Arphaxad, Shelah,”

A new sequence begins, again starting with “Shem.” This time there is no table of nations. Like verses 1–4, this section lists names only, without connecting words. The genealogy has surveyed all the families of Noah's sons; now it returns to Shem to follow the single line that leads to Abraham. “Arphaxad” and “Shelah” are repeated from verse 18. Restarting with Shem marks a deliberate narrowing of focus, from the nations of the world to the family through which God would bring His promise.
24.notes:
Verses 24–27 compress Genesis 11:10–26, as verses 1–4 compress Genesis 5. Each sequence consists of ten generations: Adam to Noah, and Shem to Abram.

This symmetry is present in Genesis and preserved in Chronicles. It does not by itself show that either list is complete.

25.brief: Eber, Peleg, and Reu continue the line. Here Peleg is followed rather than his brother Joktan, carrying the record toward Abraham.
25.explain:
“Eber, Peleg, Reu,”

The line continues through “Eber” and “Peleg.” This time the record follows Peleg rather than his brother Joktan, whose family was listed in verses 20–23. “Reu,” Peleg's son, carries the line forward (Genesis 11:18–19). By following Peleg, the genealogy moves away from the scattered nations and toward Abraham. The narrowing that began with Shem continues with each name.

26.brief: Serug, Nahor, and Terah bring the line to Abraham’s father. The sequence follows Genesis 11 without its ages and intervals.
26.explain:
“Serug, Nahor, Terah,”

Three more generations bring the line to Abraham's father. “Serug” was Reu's son, and “Nahor” was Serug's son. “Terah” was Abraham's father, who left Ur of the Chaldeans with his family and settled in Haran (Genesis 11:31). Joshua later reminded Israel that “Terah, the father of Abraham” had served other gods beyond the River (Joshua 24:2). Chronicles mentions none of this. It names the generations that led up to Abraham and moves on.
26.notes: This Nahor was Abraham's grandfather. Abraham also had a brother named Nahor (Genesis 11:26–27), whose granddaughter Rebekah became Isaac's wife (Genesis 24:15).

27.brief: The line reaches its goal in “Abram, who is Abraham” (1:27). The double name recalls the new name God gave him with His promise in Genesis 17:5, marking the turn from the nations to the family through whom that promise would be carried.
27.explain:
“and Abram, who is Abraham.”

The line reaches its goal. The record identifies Abram by his later name: “Abram, who is Abraham.” Abram was his name at birth (Genesis 11:26). God changed it to “Abraham” when He confirmed His promise, saying, “No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham; for I have made you a father of many nations” (Genesis 17:5). The double name compresses that whole story into a phrase. It recalls both who Abraham was and what God made him by His promise.

With this name the genealogy turns a corner. The chapter began with Adam and all humanity, surveyed the nations descended from Noah, and narrowed through Shem and Eber to a single man. From here the record will follow Abraham's family, and through it, Israel. Yet the earlier verses keep the nations in view. Genesis records God's promise to Abraham that “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). Chronicles does not quote that promise, but it has just listed those families.
27.notes: “Abram” is usually understood as ‘exalted father’ and “Abraham” as ‘father of a multitude,’ based on God's explanation in Genesis 17:5. The second element of Abraham's name sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘multitude.’

28.brief: Abraham’s sons are named as Isaac and Ishmael. Both sons are acknowledged before the record follows their families.
28.explain:
“The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael.”

Abraham's two sons are named. “Isaac” is listed first, although “Ishmael” was the elder, born to Hagar fourteen years before Isaac (Genesis 16:16; 21:5). The order reflects Isaac's place as the son of promise, through whom God said Abraham's line would be named (Genesis 21:12). Yet Ishmael is not left out. He is acknowledged as Abraham's son, and the next verses give his family its own record. Chronicles honors both sons before following the line through Isaac.
28.notes: Listing first the son through whom the line continues is also seen at 1:4, where Shem precedes his brothers, and in Genesis 11:26, where Abram precedes his brothers, though the birth order in those cases is not clearly stated.

29.brief: Ishmael’s genealogy begins with his firstborn Nebajoth, then Kedar, Adbeel, and Mibsam. Ishmael’s family receives its own record before attention returns to Isaac.
29.explain:
“These are their genealogies:”

This heading introduces the family records that follow. Verses 29–31 list Ishmael's sons, verses 32–33 list Keturah's descendants, and verse 34 returns to Isaac's family.

“The firstborn of Ishmael was Nebajoth; then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,”

Ishmael's family comes first. “Nebajoth” was his firstborn, and “Kedar” his second son. Kedar became a well-known Arabian people, famous for their black tents and flocks (Psalm 120:5; Song of Solomon 1:5). Isaiah envisions the flocks of Kedar and the rams of Nebajoth (spelled “Nebaioth”) brought to the LORD's altar in the age to come (Isaiah 60:7). “Adbeel” and “Mibsam” are known only from these lists. Ishmael's descendants receive a full record before attention returns to Isaac.

30.brief: Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, and Tema continue the list of Ishmael’s sons. The record keeps adding to the family God had promised to bless and multiply.
30.explain:
“Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema,”

Five more of Ishmael's sons are listed. “Dumah” and “Tema” were oases in northern Arabia; Isaiah delivers oracles concerning both (Isaiah 21:11, 14). Job speaks of “the caravans of Tema” (Job 6:19). “Massa” may be the people from which came King Lemuel's oracle in Proverbs 31:1, though that is uncertain. “Hadad” and “Mishma” are otherwise little known. Chronicles keeps adding names to the family God had promised to bless and multiply (Genesis 17:20).
30.notes: Genesis 25:15 reads “Hadar” for “Hadad.” As with other name differences in this chapter, the Hebrew letters d and r are easily confused in copying.

31.brief: The list of Ishmael’s sons ends with Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah, bringing the total to twelve. The completed number reflects God’s word that Ishmael would father twelve princes (Genesis 17:20).
31.explain:
“Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.”

The final three names complete Ishmael's family. “Jetur” is the ancestor of the Itureans, who lived in the region northeast of Galilee; Luke mentions “Iturea” in his account of the time of John the Baptist (Luke 3:1). “Naphish” appears with Jetur among peoples defeated by the tribes east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:19). “Kedemah” means ‘eastward.’

“These were the sons of Ishmael.”

The summary closes the list. Ishmael had twelve sons, just as God had promised Abraham: “He shall beget twelve princes, and I will make him a great nation” (Genesis 17:20). The completed number shows God's faithfulness to His word concerning Ishmael. God kept His promise to the son outside the line of promise as surely as He would keep His promises to Isaac.
31.notes: Genesis 25:16 calls Ishmael’s sons “twelve princes according to their nations.” Chronicles lists the names without that description.

32.brief: The sons born to Keturah, Abraham’s concubine, are listed, including Midian, together with the sons of Jokshan, Sheba and Dedan. Abraham’s wider family includes peoples who later appear in Israel’s history, such as the Midianites.
32.explain:
“Now the sons born to Keturah, Abraham's concubine, were Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.”

The list turns to another branch of Abraham's family. “Keturah” bore him six sons. Genesis calls her his wife (Genesis 25:1), and later speaks of “the sons of the concubines which Abraham had” (Genesis 25:6). Chronicles calls her “Abraham's concubine,” a wife of secondary status whose sons did not inherit with Isaac. Of her sons, “Midian” is the best known. The Midianites appear often in Israel's history: Midianite traders carried Joseph to Egypt (Genesis 37:28), Moses found refuge in Midian and married there (Exodus 2:15–21), and in the days of the judges the Midianites oppressed Israel until Gideon defeated them (Judges 6–8). “Shuah” may be the ancestor of Bildad the Shuhite, Job's friend (Job 2:11).

“The sons of Jokshan were Sheba and Dedan.”

The record notes Jokshan's two sons. These names also appear among Cush's descendants (1:9), probably because these Arabian peoples had connections with more than one branch of the human family.
32.notes:
Mesopotamian law shows a comparable ranking. Under the Code of Hammurabi (laws 170–171), children a slave woman bore to her master shared his estate only if he had acknowledged them as his own, and even then the wife’s children chose their shares first.

Genesis 25:5–6 records that Abraham gave everything to Isaac but gave gifts to the sons of the concubines and sent them east.

33.brief: Midian’s sons are named, and the verse sums up that all these were the children of Keturah. The record acknowledges this branch of Abraham’s family while keeping it distinct from Isaac’s line.
33.explain:
“The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah.”

The genealogy follows Midian into the next generation. “Ephah” appears with Midian in Isaiah's vision of nations bringing gifts and praise to the LORD: “The dromedaries of Midian and Ephah” (Isaiah 60:6). The other names are known only from these lists.

“All these were the children of Keturah.”

The summary closes Keturah's branch. Chronicles acknowledges these descendants of Abraham while keeping them distinct from Isaac's line. They are part of Abraham's family and the family of nations, but the story Chronicles will tell runs through Isaac and Israel.
33.notes: Genesis 25:3 also lists the sons of Dedan, which Chronicles omits.

34.brief: The genealogy returns to Abraham’s son Isaac and names his two sons, Esau and Israel. Calling Jacob by the name Israel points ahead to the people whose story Chronicles will tell.
34.explain:
“And Abraham begot Isaac.”

The genealogy returns to Abraham and to “Isaac,” the son of promise. The simple statement “Abraham begot Isaac” echoes the opening of the genealogy of Isaac in Genesis (Genesis 25:19). After acknowledging the other branches of Abraham's family, the record now resumes the main line.

“The sons of Isaac were Esau and Israel.”

Isaac's two sons are named. “Esau” was the elder twin and is listed first (Genesis 25:25–26). His brother is called “Israel,” the name God gave Jacob after he wrestled with Him at Peniel: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel” (Genesis 32:28). Chronicles almost always uses the name Israel for Jacob. The choice is significant. The man is identified by the name that also belongs to the people descended from him, the people whose story Chronicles tells. Esau's family will be listed first (1:35–54), and then the sons of Israel (2:1).
34.notes: In Chronicles the name “Jacob” occurs only in the psalm of 1 Chronicles 16:13, 17.

35.brief: Esau’s sons are listed: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah. Before following Israel, the record gives Esau’s family its place, as Genesis 36 does.
35.explain:
“The sons of Esau were Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah.”

Esau's family is listed first. Genesis records that Esau had three wives and five sons. “Eliphaz” was born to Adah, “Reuel” to Basemath, and “Jeush,” “Jaalam,” and “Korah” to Aholibamah (Genesis 36:4–5). Chronicles names the sons without their mothers. Esau is identified with Edom (Genesis 36:1, 8), and his descendants became the Edomites, Israel's neighbors to the southeast. Their relationship with Israel was often hostile, yet the record gives Esau's family its place, as Genesis 36 does. God had blessed Esau too, giving him Mount Seir as a possession (Deuteronomy 2:5).
35.notes: This Korah, Esau's son, is unrelated to Korah the Levite who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16) and whose descendants are named in the titles of several psalms.

36.brief: The sons of Eliphaz are named, and Amalek is recorded as born by Timna. The notice includes Amalek, whose descendants would become persistent enemies of Israel.
36.explain:
“And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, and Kenaz;”

The list follows Esau's firstborn, “Eliphaz,” into the next generation. “Teman” became the name of a region in Edom famed for wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7). Job's friend was “Eliphaz the Temanite” (Job 2:11). “Kenaz” gave his name to a clan; the Kenezzites appear among the peoples of the land (Genesis 15:19), and Caleb is called a Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12), though the relationship to Esau's grandson is uncertain. “Omar,” “Zephi,” and “Gatam” are otherwise unknown.

“and by Timna, Amalek.”

The last name is significant. “Amalek” became the ancestor of the Amalekites, Israel's persistent enemies. Shortly after the exodus they attacked Israel in the wilderness, and the LORD declared, “the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation” (Exodus 17:16). Saul was later rejected for failing to carry out God's judgment on them (1 Samuel 15). The note “by Timna” identifies Amalek's mother. Genesis explains that Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz (Genesis 36:12). The record includes Amalek within Esau's family without comment, but readers who knew Israel's history would recognize the name.
36.notes:
The Hebrew reads literally ‘and Timna and Amalek,’ which could appear to list Timna as another son of Eliphaz. The Latin Vulgate reads it that way, as do the KJV and NASB among English versions.

The NKJV supplies “by,” following Genesis 36:12.

Genesis 36:11 reads “Zepho” for “Zephi.”

Chronicles itself records that men of Simeon later destroyed “the rest of the Amalekites who had escaped” (1 Chronicles 4:43).

37.brief: Reuel’s sons are Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. With them the record of Esau’s grandsons is complete.
37.explain:
“The sons of Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.”

The genealogy now follows Esau's second son, “Reuel,” whose mother was Basemath, Ishmael's daughter (Genesis 36:3–4). His four sons are named as in Genesis 36:13. Several of them later appear as chiefs of Edomite clans (Genesis 36:17). With them, the record of Esau's grandsons is complete. Chronicles does not trace the lines of Esau's other three sons. Its purpose is to acknowledge Esau's family, not to give a complete account of Edom.
37.notes: This Reuel, Esau's son, is a different man from Reuel the priest of Midian, Moses's father-in-law (Exodus 2:18), who is also called Jethro. The Zerah named here is distinct from Zerah the son of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:4).

38.brief: The sons of Seir are listed, beginning with Lotan, Shobal, and Zibeon. These are the families of Seir, the region where Esau settled, distinct from Esau’s own descendants though connected with them (Genesis 36:20–30).
38.explain:
“The sons of Seir were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.”

Chronicles now turns to a different family. “Seir” was the ancestor of the people who lived in the mountainous region of Seir before Esau's descendants settled there. Genesis calls him “Seir the Horite who inhabited the land” (Genesis 36:20). His seven sons were the heads of the Horite clans (Genesis 36:21). They were not Esau's descendants. Deuteronomy explains that the Horites formerly lived in Seir, “but the descendants of Esau dispossessed them” (Deuteronomy 2:12). Yet the two families became connected through marriage, and Edom's history includes them both. Chronicles places Seir's family alongside Esau's because together they make up the people of the region.

39.brief: Lotan’s sons are Hori and Homam, and Lotan’s sister is named as Timna. The name Timna also appears in verse 36, one of the links Genesis 36 shows between the families of Seir and of Esau.
39.explain:
“And the sons of Lotan were Hori and Homam;”

The list follows Lotan, the first son of Seir named in verse 38. His sons were “Hori,” whose name resembles the name of the Horites, and “Homam.”

“Lotan's sister was Timna.”

The verse adds a notice about Lotan's sister “Timna.” The name also appears in verse 36, where Amalek's mother is identified as Timna. Genesis does not explicitly say that they were the same woman, but many interpreters see her as the link between Seir's Horite family and Esau's family: a Horite woman who became the concubine of Esau's son Eliphaz. If so, her mention here explains how the two families were joined.
39.notes:
Genesis 36:22 reads “Hemam” for “Homam.”

Chief Timnah among the chiefs of Edom (1:51) may represent a clan name related to Timna, though this is unproven.

40.brief: The sons of Shobal and the sons of Zibeon are listed, continuing the record of Seir’s clans. Each family head is remembered by name within the history of the region.
40.explain:
“The sons of Shobal were Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam.”

The record continues with Seir's second son, “Shobal.” His five sons are named. “Manahath” may be connected with a place name (compare 1 Chronicles 8:6). The others are otherwise unknown. This Shobal should be distinguished from Shobal the son of Caleb in Judah's genealogy (1 Chronicles 2:50).

“The sons of Zibeon were Ajah and Anah.”

Seir's third son, “Zibeon,” had two sons. Genesis adds that this “Anah” found water (or hot springs) in the wilderness while pasturing his father's donkeys (Genesis 36:24). Chronicles does not repeat that detail. Each family head is remembered by name.
40.notes:
Genesis 36:23 reads “Alvan” for “Alian” and “Shepho” for “Shephi.”

Genesis 36:20 lists Anah as a son of Seir, and Genesis 36:24 lists Anah as a son of Zibeon, Seir's son. Chronicles preserves both (1:38, 40). They may be uncle and nephew sharing a name.

Aholibamah, Esau's wife, is called “the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon” (Genesis 36:2), linking her to this branch.

41.brief: Anah’s son Dishon is named, followed by Dishon’s four sons. The record traces this branch of Seir’s family through another generation.
41.explain:
“The son of Anah was Dishon.”

The genealogy follows “Anah,” probably the son of Seir named in verse 38. His son “Dishon” shares the name of Anah's brother Dishon (1:38). Genesis 36:25 also names a daughter, Aholibamah, who became Esau's wife. Chronicles names only the son.

“The sons of Dishon were Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.”

Chronicles traces this branch through another generation. The four names are otherwise unknown. Whether this Dishon is Anah's son or Seir's son named in verse 38 is uncertain; Genesis lists the same four sons under Dishon without further identification (Genesis 36:26). Chronicles records the names without explaining which Dishon is meant.
41.notes: Genesis 36:26 reads “Hemdan” for “Hamran.” The Hebrew letters d and r again explain the difference, together with a vowel change.

42.brief: The sons of Ezer and of Dishan complete the families of Seir. With this verse the record of the peoples of Seir comes to a close.
42.explain:
“The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan.”

Seir's sixth son, “Ezer,” had three sons. The name “Jaakan” may be connected with “Bene Jaakan,” a camping place of Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 33:31–32; compare Deuteronomy 10:6).

“The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran.”

Seir's seventh son, “Dishan,” had two sons. This “Uz” is a Horite and should be distinguished from Uz the son of Aram (1:17). With this verse the record of Seir's families is complete. The Horite clans that once held Seir are remembered by name, even though Esau's descendants later dispossessed them.
42.notes:
Genesis 36:27 reads “Akan” for “Jaakan.”

Job lived “in the land of Uz” (Job 1:1), and Lamentations 4:21 associates Uz with Edom. Whether the land of Uz is connected with the Horite Uz named here or with Uz the son of Aram is uncertain.

43.brief: The kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over the children of Israel are introduced, beginning with Bela the son of Beor, whose city was Dinhabah. The notice gives relative order, not a date, and anticipates the book’s later concern with Israel’s own kingship.
43.explain:
“Now these were the kings who reigned in the land of Edom”

The record turns from family lists to a list of rulers. “The land of Edom” was the territory south and east of the Dead Sea, including Mount Seir. Edom had a form of kingship early in its history. Moses sent messengers to “the king of Edom” when Israel sought passage through his land (Numbers 20:14).

“before a king reigned over the children of Israel:”

This phrase gives the list its significance for Chronicles. Edom had kings long before Israel did. The words look back from a time when Israel had kings, and they anticipate the book's central concern with Israel's own kingship under David and his house. God had promised Abraham and Jacob that kings would come from them (Genesis 17:6; 35:11). The note does not imply that Edom was more blessed because it had kings first. It simply gives the relative order of events and prepares the reader for the story of Israel's kingdom.

“Bela the son of Beor, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.”

The first king was “Bela the son of Beor,” who ruled from “Dinhabah.” The location of Dinhabah is unknown. Each king is identified by his father or his city.
43.notes:
The phrase parallels Genesis 36:31, which reads “before any king reigned over the children of Israel.”

Bela the son of Beor is not identified in Scripture with Balaam the son of Beor, the prophet hired by Balak (Numbers 22:5), though the similarity of the names has led some interpreters to connect them.

44.brief: When Bela dies, Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigns in his place. The succession is not presented as passing from father to son, for each king is identified by his own father or city.
44.explain:
“And when Bela died, Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.”

The second king, “Jobab the son of Zerah,” came from “Bozrah.” Bozrah was one of Edom's principal cities, later the target of prophetic judgment (Isaiah 34:6; Jeremiah 49:13). Isaiah pictures the LORD coming from Edom “With dyed garments from Bozrah” (Isaiah 63:1). The succession is not presented as passing from father to son. Jobab was a different man from a different city. The verse marks the orderly succession of Edom's rulers, each recorded in turn.
44.notes:
An addition at the end of the Greek (Septuagint) book of Job, attributed there to a Syriac source, identifies Job with Jobab and lists him among the kings of Edom. The identification comes from that Greek addition; the Hebrew text of Job and Chronicles does not make it.

This Zerah may be the son of Reuel named in verse 37, though that is not stated.

45.brief: When Jobab dies, Husham of the land of the Temanites reigns in his place as the third king in Edom’s succession.
45.explain:
“When Jobab died, Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.”

The third king was “Husham,” identified by his region rather than his father. “The land of the Temanites” was the region of Teman in Edom, named after Teman the son of Eliphaz (1:36). The area was known for its wise men (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8–9). Husham's reign continues the succession without comment. The list records Edom's rulers in order, giving each king his place in the history.

46.brief: Hadad the son of Bedad succeeds Husham and is remembered for attacking Midian in the field of Moab; his city was Avith. This king receives a brief note of a military exploit within the list.
46.explain:
“And when Husham died, Hadad the son of Bedad,”

The fourth king was “Hadad the son of Bedad.” The name Hadad was also the name of a storm god worshiped in Syria, and several later kings in the region bore names connected with it.

“who attacked Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his place.”

Hadad is the only king in the list remembered for a deed. He “attacked Midian in the field of Moab,” a military victory over the Midianites in the open country of Moab, the region east of the Dead Sea. The notice shows that the peoples listed earlier in this chapter, Midian among Abraham's sons (1:32) and Edom among Isaac's, had real dealings with one another, including war. History did not stop with the genealogies; the families became nations with their own conflicts.

“The name of his city was Avith.”

Hadad ruled from “Avith,” whose location is unknown.
46.notes:
The Midianites were largely nomadic tribes whose homeland is usually placed east of the Gulf of Aqaba in northwestern Arabia. Their presence in Moab is consistent with Numbers 22:4–7, where the elders of Moab and Midian act together against Israel.

This Hadad is different from the later king Hadad (1:50) and from Hadad the Edomite, Solomon's adversary (1 Kings 11:14), who was “a descendant of the king in Edom.”

47.brief: When Hadad dies, Samlah of Masrekah reigns in his place. Like several others in the list, he is identified only by his town.
47.explain:
“When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.”

The fifth king was “Samlah,” identified only by his town, “Masrekah.” Its location is unknown. Like several others in the list, Samlah is remembered by his origin rather than his father's name. The steady repetition of “reigned in his place” gives the list its rhythm. Each king rose, ruled, and died, and another took his place. The genealogy shows real history unfolding generation after generation in a nation neighboring Israel.

48.brief: When Samlah dies, Saul of Rehoboth-by-the-River reigns in his place. This Edomite king shares a name with Israel’s first king but is a different man.
48.explain:
“And when Samlah died, Saul of Rehoboth-by-the-River reigned in his place.”

The sixth king was “Saul,” from “Rehoboth-by-the-River.” He shares a name with Israel's first king but is a different man entirely. The name means ‘asked for.’ His town's name means ‘broad places by the river.’ “The River” in the Old Testament usually refers to the Euphrates, but a town that far north seems unlikely for an Edomite king, and some suggest a river or streambed within Edom is meant. The location remains uncertain.

49.brief: When Saul dies, Baal-Hanan the son of Achbor reigns in his place. He is identified by his father’s name rather than by a city.
49.explain:
“When Saul died, Baal-Hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.”

The seventh king was “Baal-Hanan the son of Achbor.” He is identified by his father's name rather than a city. His name means ‘Baal is gracious,’ reflecting the worship of Baal common among the peoples around Israel. The list records his reign without comment on his religion or character. Chronicles includes these kings as historical rulers, not as examples to be followed or condemned.
49.notes: Another Baal-Hanan, a Gederite, served as David's official over olive and sycamore trees (1 Chronicles 27:28). The names are the same; the men are different.

50.brief: When Baal-Hanan dies, Hadad reigns from the city of Pai, and his wife Mehetabel is named with her ancestry. The last king in the list receives a fuller note that also remembers the queen’s family.
50.explain:
“And when Baal-Hanan died, Hadad reigned in his place;”

The eighth and last king was “Hadad,” a second king of that name in the list.

“and the name of his city was Pai.”

He ruled from “Pai,” another town whose location is unknown.

“His wife's name was Mehetabel the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.”

The last king receives a fuller family notice. His wife, “Mehetabel,” is named as the daughter of “Matred,” with “Mezahab” also named in her ancestry. The wording preserves the queen's family connections alongside the king's city. It does not identify Mezahab as a woman. Mehetabel's name means ‘God does good.’
50.notes: Genesis 36:39 reads “Hadar” for “Hadad” and “Pau” for “Pai.” The first difference involves the similar Hebrew letters represented by d and r. “Pai” and “Pau” also end with different Hebrew letters: yod in Chronicles and vav in Genesis.

51.brief: Hadad’s death is noted, and the record turns to the chiefs of Edom, beginning with Timnah, Aliah, and Jetheth. Edom’s history is summarized through both its kings and its clan chiefs.
51.explain:
“Hadad died also.”

The list of kings closes with the death of the last king. Genesis 36:39 does not record Hadad's death; Chronicles adds this note, completing the list. Whether the note implies that kingship in Edom ended with Hadad, or simply rounds off the record, is not stated.

“And the chiefs of Edom were Chief Timnah, Chief Aliah, Chief Jetheth,”

Chronicles turns to the “chiefs of Edom.” The word “Chief” refers to the head of a clan or tribal division. Genesis introduces this list as “the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their families and their places, by their names” (Genesis 36:40). The names may refer both to clan leaders and to the clans or regions they led. “Timnah” recalls Timna, Lotan's sister and Amalek's mother (1:36, 39). “Aliah” and “Jetheth” are otherwise unknown. Edom's history is summarized through both its kings and its clan chiefs.
51.notes:
“Chief” translates the Hebrew word alluph, used especially for Edom's clan leaders (Genesis 36:15–43; Exodus 15:15).

Genesis 36:40 reads “Alvah” for “Aliah.”

Whether the chiefs ruled after the kings, alongside them, or in different regions is not clear.

52.brief: Aholibamah, Elah, and Pinon follow among the chiefs of Edom, leaders identified by title rather than by any reign or city.
52.explain:
“Chief Aholibamah, Chief Elah, Chief Pinon,”

Three more chiefs of Edom are named. “Aholibamah” is also the name of one of Esau's wives, the daughter of Anah (Genesis 36:2). Here it appears as the name of a chief or clan, possibly a clan named after her. “Elah” and “Pinon” are otherwise unknown, though Pinon has been connected with Punon, a camping place of Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 33:42). These leaders are identified by title rather than by reign or city. The list continues to name the leaders who shaped Edom's history.

53.brief: The chiefs Kenaz, Teman, and Mibzar are added. Kenaz and Teman also appear among Esau’s descendants in verse 36, linking Edom’s chiefs with Esau’s family.
53.explain:
“Chief Kenaz, Chief Teman, Chief Mibzar,”

Three more chiefs complete the next part of the list. “Kenaz” and “Teman” also appear among the sons of Eliphaz, Esau's son (1:36). Their appearance here links Edom's chiefs with Esau's family, showing that the clans took their names from his descendants. “Mibzar” means ‘fortress’ and may be a place name. The overlap of names between the genealogy and the list of chiefs shows how families became clans and clans became regions in Edom's history.

54.brief: The list ends with Magdiel and Iram and the summary, “These were the chiefs of Edom.” With Edom’s record complete, the genealogy is ready to turn to the sons of Israel.
54.explain:
“Chief Magdiel, and Chief Iram.”

The last two chiefs are named. Magdiel and Iram also appear in Genesis 36:43, but these parallel lists supply no further personal history.

“These were the chiefs of Edom.”

The summary closes Edom's record. The chapter that began with “Adam” (1:1) ends with the leaders of Edom. Between them, Chronicles has surveyed all humanity, the families of Noah's sons, the line from Shem to Abraham, and the families of Abraham, Ishmael, Keturah, Esau, and Seir. Edom's record is given in full before the genealogy turns to Israel. The next verse will begin, “These were the sons of Israel” (2:1). Esau's family has received its place; now the record follows Israel.
54.notes:
Completing the record of Esau before turning to Israel matches Genesis, where Esau's genealogy in Genesis 36 precedes the story of Jacob's sons in Genesis 37.

David later subdued Edom (1 Chronicles 18:12–13).
